p74: 74.  The Government considered that those principles had to be applied in such a way as to strike the greatest possible balance between the rights of each of the parents and those of the child. They nevertheless pointed to the difficulty of the task facing the national authorities when confronted with international child abductions, which did not always make it possible to protect the best interests of all the parties, especially those of the child, since each party had a definition of those interests that differed from, or even contradicted, that of the others. Furthermore, they stressed that a clear distinction had to be made between return proceedings and custody proceedings.
p75: 75.  The Government considered that the national authorities enjoyed a margin of appreciation in applying those principles to the circumstances of the case. The Court’s task was not to enter into the details of the domestic proceedings but to ascertain whether the decision-making process, seen as a whole, had enabled those concerned to assert their rights fully (see Diamante and Pelliccioni v. San Marino, no. 32250/08, § 187, 27 September 2011), since the Court was not a court of fourth instance. Accordingly, the position could be otherwise only if the shortcomings observed had been decisive for the outcome of the proceedings (see Broka v. Latvia, no. 70926/01, §§ 25-26, 28 June 2007).
p76: 76.  In the present case, they were of the view that the national authorities had complied with those principles and had carried out an “in-depth examination of the entire family situation and of a whole series of factors” (see Neulinger and Shuruk, cited above, § 139), but that the extent to which the entire family situation was taken into account had to vary from case to case, depending on whether or not there were obvious causes for concern or at least reasonable doubts. Moreover, the risk provided for in Article 13 (b) had to be “grave”, in addition to which the best interests of the child also required a speedy procedure.
p77: 77.  The Government stated that the request sent by the Australian authorities to the Latvian authorities on 15 September 2008 attested to the fact that T. had been exercising joint parental responsibility for the child and that, contrary to the applicant’s submissions, the judgment of 6 November 2008 had not conferred that right on T. but had confirmed that it existed at the time of his daughter’s departure from Australia. Both the Australian and the Latvian courts had established that T. had actually been exercising his parental responsibilities, that there was sufficient evidence to presume that T. was the child’s biological father and that the applicant, for her part, had made false statements to the authorities in order to obtain benefits.
p78: 78.  They stated that the expert report had been drawn up privately at the applicant’s request and that the “Bāriņtiesa” was not a judicial institution. Notwithstanding the rejection of that report and of the observations of the “Bāriņtiesa”, the courts had examined the family situation in the light of the evidence before them, which was within their competence, and nothing in the Court’s case-law could call that power into question. The Latvian courts had found that the applicant’s departure from Australia with her daughter had been motivated solely by her personal disagreement with T. and that there was no appearance of a risk to the child in the event of her return: accordingly, the Latvian authorities had not applied the Hague Convention automatically or mechanically, in disregard of the principles laid down by Article 8 of the Convention.
p79: 79.  The Government emphasised that “the understanding and cooperation of all concerned are always an important ingredient” in assessing the particular circumstances of a case (see Maumousseau and Washington, cited above, § 83, and Neulinger and Shuruk, cited above, § 140). They considered that the applicant had shown a lack of cooperation with the Australian and Latvian authorities by ignoring the invitation to take part in the proceedings before the Australian court, by preventing the representatives of the “Bāriņtiesa” from verifying her living conditions with her daughter in Latvia, by obstructing contact between T. and his daughter and through her extremely aggressive attitude towards T. during the proceedings.
p80: 80.  They also considered that the courts had rightly disregarded the issue of the child’s integration into her new environment, since she had spent only a few months in Latvia.
p81: 81.  They noted that the courts had not ordered the child’s return to her father, but her return to Australia, thus making a clear distinction between the return and the custody of the child, an approach which had been endorsed by the Court (see M.R. and L.R. v. Estonia (dec.), no. 13420/12, §§ 47-48, 15 May 2012, and Tarkhova v. Ukraine (dec.), no. 8984/11, 6 September 2011). In any event, T.’s financial situation was not such as to prevent him from taking care of his daughter.
